worked_examples.problem: In-Text Question (Section 4.1 & 4.2, p. 4 & p. 11): (a) Draw the electron dot structures of: Carbon dioxide (CO2), Methane (CH4), and Nitrogen molecule (N2). (b) What are the two unique properties of carbon that lead to the formation of a huge variety of organic compounds?
worked_examples.given: Covalent bonding in carbon; Valency and electronic configuration.
worked_examples.formula: Octet rule; Catenation (self-linking via strong C-C covalent bonds) and Tetravalency.
worked_examples.substitution: Carbon shares 4 valence electrons; N shares 3 pairs (triple bond); O shares 2 pairs with C (double bonds).
worked_examples.calculation:
(a) Electron Dot Structures:
1. Methane (CH4): Central C shares 1 electron pair each with 4 H atoms (4 single C-H covalent bonds).
2. Carbon dioxide (CO2): Central C forms double covalent bonds with two O atoms: O=C=O (4 shared electron pairs).
3. Nitrogen (N2): Two N atoms share three electron pairs forming a stable triple bond (:N≡N:).
(b) Two properties:
1. CATENATION: The unique ability of carbon to form strong, stable covalent bonds with other carbon atoms to form straight chains, branched networks, and rings.
2. TETRAVALENCY: Having 4 valence electrons, carbon bonds with H, O, N, halogens, creating immense functional diversity.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) CO2 has double bonds (O=C=O), CH4 has 4 single C-H bonds, N2 has a triple bond (:N≡N:); (b) Catenation and Tetravalency.

worked_examples.problem: End-of-Chapter Exercise Q6, Q7, Q8 (p. 20): (a) How can ethanol and ethanoic acid be differentiated on the basis of their physical and chemical properties? (b) Explain the cleansing action of soaps with a micelle diagram.
worked_examples.given: Ethanol (C2H5OH) vs Ethanoic acid (CH3COOH); Soap surfactant cleansing mechanics.
worked_examples.formula: Esterification, carbonate effervescence: 2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 -> 2CH3COONa + H2O + CO2; Soap micelle hydrophilic head and hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail.
worked_examples.substitution: Contrast chemical reactions and micelle formation.
worked_examples.calculation:
(a) Distinguishing Tests:
1. Sodium hydrogen carbonate test: Ethanoic acid reacts with NaHCO3 with brisk effervescence liberating CO2 gas (turns lime water milky). Ethanol does not react.
2. Litmus test: Ethanoic acid turns blue litmus red. Ethanol is neutral and causes no color change.
(b) Cleansing Action of Soap:
Soap molecules are sodium/potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids (e.g. C17H35COONa). They have two distinct ends: a hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail and a hydrophilic ionic carboxylate head (COO- Na+). In water containing greasy dirt, the hydrophobic tails dissolve into the oil droplet while ionic heads orient outward facing polar water. This forms spherical clusters called MICELLES that trap dirt in the center, allowing it to be rinsed away as an emulsion.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) Ethanoic acid gives brisk effervescence with NaHCO3 and turns blue litmus red; ethanol does not; (b) Soap forms micelles with hydrophobic tails trapping oil inside and hydrophilic heads facing water.
